title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 22: Introductions
keywords: Chevalier of the National Order of Merit of France
Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry
primary_topics: Chapter 22 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- three speaker introductions CJP delivered between 1989 and 1993, showing the form he used as 'a sought-after introducer of guest speakers': national history first, then personal acquaintance, then a catalogue of achievement, then a moral portrait, and finally the name

The introduction of Senate President Jovito R. Salonga (March 15, 1989), placing him in a line of crisis-born Filipino leaders from Rizal and Mabini to Laurel and Recto, and presenting him as a man whose record of topping every contest is matched by an almost ascetic personal life

The introduction of Maximo V. Soliven (September 30, 1992), a 'many-splendored career' told through partial truths -- most outstanding journalist, most famous publishing CEO -- and climaxing in his martial-law imprisonment as Ninoy Aquino's cellmate and the writing ban that pained him most

The introduction of Dr. Jesus P. Estanislao (December 14, 1993), presented as proof against those who dispute 'the possibility of pursuing the holiness of God while achieving excellence in one's chosen career' -- a technocrat's résumé framed by sanctity and unquestioned integrity
sub_topics: The editor's note explains that Panganiban was as sought after to introduce guest speakers as he was as a main speaker, and offers three samples

Salonga: CJP opens on the national frame -- in every crisis 'men of integrity, wisdom and courage rise up undaunted and unafraid,' from Rizal and Mabini in the Revolution to Laurel and Recto after World War II, and now, after 'an epic battle against a corrupt and decadent dictatorship,' the guest speaker

He declines to read the distributed curriculum vitae and instead introduces Salonga as he personally knew him -- his professor and dean in law school 30 years earlier, his first boss after graduation, the man whose teaching chores at Far Eastern University he took over, and a career he has 'assiduously admired and cherished'
He describes the effect of the man -- still 'mesmerized and awed' by his presence, and a 'forceful tremolo' that spellbinds hearers 'with his wisdom, sincerity, honesty and credibility'

He lists the firsts: topping the 1943 bar, the Ambrose Gherini Prize from Yale Law School for the best paper in international law, and topping the senatorial elections three times -- 1965, 1971 and 1987 -- a feat no one had achieved

He cites the PCGG test: while Salonga headed the Presidential Commission on Good Government, 'the vaunted money, men and machines of Marcos and his cronies' were used to defile him, yet his reputation 'remained unblemished and ever immaculate'
He sketches the private man -- dedicated husband, caring father, devoted man of God, who does not smoke, drink or gamble and does not even own the house he lives in at Pasig

He retells Plaza Miranda: at the 1971 Liberal Party miting de avance a grenade killed eight and drove a thousand pieces of shrapnel into Salonga, whose blood pressure fell to zero, yet who recovered with his 'towering intellect' intact and asked, 'There must be a reason why God spared my life'

Soliven: CJP calls him 'a legend of our time' and builds the introduction on partial truths -- the longest and most persuasive English-language column six days a week, a daily Tagalog column, and past work for Newsweek, the New York Times, the South China Morning Post, the Bangkok Post and others

He lists the publishing offices: publisher and editorial-board chairman of the Philippine Star, chairman and editor in chief of Eastgate International (publisher of Mabuhay), founding publisher in 1985 of the Philippine Daily Inquirer 'established to fight the Marcos dictatorship,' and, at 27, the youngest publisher and editor-in-chief of the pre-martial law Evening News

He catalogues honors and encounters -- National Press Club, Catholic Mass Media Awards, Rotary Club of Manila, and Chevalier of the National Order of Merit of France from President Francois Mitterand; interviews with Deng Xiao Ping, Nehru, Rajiv Gandhi, Kennedy, Sukarno, Golda Meir and Japanese premiers; and expulsions by Ngo Dinh Diem, Ne Win and Lee Kuan Yew

He names the 'trouble' that makes Soliven 'an authentic hero of our time': arrest and maximum-security detention as Ninoy Aquino's cellmate, then three years confined to Metro Manila, seven years barred from foreign travel and seven years forbidden to write or give interviews -- the last prohibition, CJP judges, the one that truly pained him
He adds the political refusal: every party but Marcos' KBL tried to draft him, but 'he says he has not lost his sanity yet'

Estanislao: CJP presents him as 'the epitome of a God-loving person and model public servant' and living proof 'that indeed, one can be a saint in the midst of the noise and banging of the world,' having forsaken worldly possessions and 'marital security'

He runs the résumé -- University of San Carlos, Fordham and a Harvard doctorate in economics; president of the AFTA Advisory Commission and the Southeast Asian Science Foundation; secretary of finance 1990-1992 and concurrent chairman of the Land Bank

He adds the private-sector chairmanships and directorships and the academic posts (UP professorial lecturer, professor of economic policy at the Center for Research and Communication, teaching fellow at Harvard), closing on the point that nothing in his career 'placed his integrity or judgment in doubt'

stances.claim: Filipino history shows that in every crisis 'men of integrity, wisdom and courage rise up undaunted and unafraid,' and Salonga stands in that succession after the fall of the dictatorship.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical-succession framing: Rizal and Mabini, then Laurel and Recto, then the guest speaker, so the introduction arrives as the next chapter of a national pattern

stances.claim: Salonga's integrity is proven rather than asserted: he topped the bar, won Yale's Ambrose Gherini Prize, topped the senatorial elections three times, and emerged from the PCGG with a reputation 'unblemished and ever immaculate' despite the money and machines arrayed against him.
stances.rhetorical_move: record-as-proof, sealed by an ascetic private portrait (no smoking, drinking or gambling; not even owning his house) and by the Plaza Miranda survival read as providence

stances.claim: Soliven is 'an authentic hero of our time' less for his awards than for his imprisonment under martial law and the seven-year ban on writing, the prohibition that truly pained a man who 'cannot be stopped from writing and speaking.'
stances.rhetorical_move: partial-truth structure -- each superlative conceded as 'only a partial truth. But a truth nonetheless' -- so the real claim lands at the end

stances.claim: Holiness and professional excellence are compatible: against those who 'have disputed the possibility of pursuing the holiness of God while achieving excellence in one's chosen career,' Estanislao is 'a quiet, living, day-to-day witness' that 'one can be a saint in the midst of the noise and banging of the world.'
stances.rhetorical_move: counter-example to a stated objection, with the résumé introduced only after the moral claim has been made

notable_anecdotes: Student, employee, successor: CJP introduces Salonga as his law professor and dean 30 years earlier, his first boss after graduation, and the man whose Far Eastern University teaching chores he took over.
Still awed: despite years of exposure to him, CJP says he remains 'mesmerized and awed' by Salonga's presence and his 'forceful tremolo.'

Plaza Miranda: he retells the 1971 grenade attack that killed eight and left Salonga with a thousand pieces of shrapnel and a blood pressure of zero, who woke reflecting, 'There must be a reason why God spared my life.'
The house he does not own: he notes Salonga does not smoke, drink or gamble, and 'does not even own the house where he stays in Pasig, his hometown.'
Cellmate of Ninoy: he names Soliven's arrest and maximum-security detention as Ninoy Aquino's cellmate as the 'trouble' that makes him an authentic hero, followed by bans on travel and writing.
Thrown out of three countries: he lists Soliven's expulsions from South Vietnam by Ngo Dinh Diem, from Burma by Ne Win and from Singapore by Lee Kuan Yew.
Refusing office: he reports that every party but Marcos' KBL courted Soliven, but 'he says he has not lost his sanity yet.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Love God, Serve Man' collects three speaker introductions Artemio V. Panganiban delivered between 1989 and 1993, prefaced by an editor's note calling him as sought after an introducer as he was a main speaker. The first, for Senate President Jovito R. Salonga at the Century Park Sheraton on March 15, 1989, opened on national history -- in every crisis 'men of integrity, wisdom and courage rise up undaunted and unafraid,' Rizal and Mabini, then Laurel and Recto, and now, after 'an epic battle against a corrupt and decadent dictatorship,' the guest. Declining to read the distributed curriculum vitae, CJP introduced Salonga as he personally knew him: his law professor and dean 30 years earlier, his first boss, and the man whose Far Eastern University teaching he took over. He described a 'forceful tremolo' that spellbinds hearers, listed the firsts -- topping the 1943 bar, Yale's Ambrose Gherini Prize, and topping the senatorial elections in 1965, 1971 and 1987 -- and noted that at the Presidential Commission on Good Government 'the vaunted money, men and machines of Marcos and his cronies' failed to defile a reputation that 'remained unblemished and ever immaculate.' He sketched an ascetic private life -- a man who does not smoke, drink or gamble and does not even own his house in Pasig -- and retold the 1971 Plaza Miranda grenade attack that left Salonga with a thousand shrapnel wounds, who woke asking, 'There must be a reason why God spared my life.' The second, for Maximo V. Soliven on September 30, 1992, called him 'a legend of our time' with a 'many-splendored career,' each superlative conceded as 'only a partial truth. But a truth nonetheless': the longest English-language column six days a week, work for Newsweek and the New York Times, the Philippine Star, the founding of the Philippine Daily Inquirer in 1985 to fight the dictatorship, and, at 27, the pre-martial law Evening News. After the awards, the French knighthood, the interviews with world leaders and the expulsions by Ngo Dinh Diem, Ne Win and Lee Kuan Yew, CJP located the real heroism in Soliven's maximum-security detention as Ninoy Aquino's cellmate and the seven-year writing ban that pained him most. The third, for Dr. Jesus P. Estanislao before the 19th Philippine Business Conference on December 14, 1993, presented him as 'the epitome of a God-loving person and model public servant' and living proof that 'one can be a saint in the midst of the noise and banging of the world,' before running his degrees, his term as secretary of finance and his academic posts, and concluding that nothing in his career had ever placed his integrity or judgment in doubt.
